'''tuck<sup>3</sup>''' (tuk), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tuk'' (Sc. ''tuick'', ''touk''), < OF. ''estoc'', a thrust, = OIt. ''tocco'', a knock, stroke, as on a bell, peal of a bell; cf. ''tuck''<sup>2</sup>, ''tucket''<sup>1</sup>, and ''tick''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A blow; a stroke; a tap; a beat; especially, the beating of a drum. See ''beat'' or ''tuck of drum'', under ''beat''<sup>1</sup>. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Hercules it smytis with ane mychty ''touk''.
{{right|''G. Douglas'', tr. of Virgil, p. 249.}}
<poem>Panmuir with all his men did cum,
The provost of braif Aberdene,
With trumpets and with ''tuick'' of drum,
Came schortly in thair armour schene.</poem>
{{right|''Battle of Harlaw'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 185).}}
<poem>So gallantly you come,
I read you for a bold Dragoon,
That lists the ''tuck'' of drum.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, iii. 17.}}}}
'''2.''' A blast; a flourish; a tucket.
{{smaller block|<poem>With the ''tuk'' of a trump, all his tore knightes
He assemblit full sone.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7107.}}
Wherever death has his red flag a flying, and sounds his own potent ''tuck'' upon the cannons.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Inland Voyage, p. 101.}}}}

'''tuck<sup>3</sup>''' (tuk), ''v. i.'' [< ''tuck''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.''] To beat; tap: said of a drum.
{{smaller block|<poem>The armies met, the trumpet sounds,
The dandring drums alloud did ''touk''.</poem>
{{right|''Battle of Harlaw'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 186).}}}}

{{RunningHeader|tub-wheel|6522|'''tucker'''}}{{nop}}'''tub-wheel''' (tub′hwēl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A form of water-wheel which has a vertical axis and radial spiral floats placed between two cases attached to the axis. The water is precipitated between the cases from a chute, and is discharged at the bottom of the wheel. ''E. H. Knight.''—'''2.''' In ''tanning'', a hollow revolving drum in which skins or leather are washed by being tumbled in water. Similar wheels are used in other industries. [[File:century v08 p0326 c1f1.png|center|108px]] {{c|{{smaller|Tub-wheel, 1.}}}} '''tucan''' (tö′ka̤n), ''n.'' [< Mex. ''tucan'' (Hernandez).] The Mexican pocket-gopher, ''Geomys mexicanus.'' {{smaller|It is one of the largest gophers, 10 or 11 inches long, or, with the tail, from 13 to 14 inches, and resembles the quachil, but has soft, sleek fur. The incisors are each bisected by a single median furrow, which distinguishes the animal from all United States gophers except ''G. castanops.'' The tail and feet are clothed as usual in the genus. The coloration is a pure chestnut-brown, the hind feet and tail are mostly whitish, and sometimes there are small white patches on the under parts. The under fur is plumbeous, and some specimens vary from the normal chestnut to a plumbago or anthracite color. Also ''tugan, tuca, tuza.''}} '''Tucana''' (tū-kā′nä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < ''toucan'', q. v.] '''1.''' A southern constellation, the Toucan, south of the Phœnix, made by Petrus Theodori in the fifteenth century.—'''2.''' In ''ornith.'', same as ''Ramphastos. Brisson'', 1760. '''tucet†''' (tū′set), ''n.'' [< L. ''tucetum, tuccetum'', a thick gravy: see ''tucket''2.] A steak. See ''tucket''2. {{smaller block|The Cisalpine ''tucets'' or gobbets of condited bull’s flesh. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Sermons (1653), p. 212. (''Latham.'')}}}} '''tuch†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''touch''. '''tuck1''' (tuk), ''v.'' [< ME. ''tucken'', ''tukken'', also ''touken''; partly < AS. ''tucian'', pull, pluck, full (cloth); partly < MLG. ''tucken'', LG. ''tukken'', ''tokken'', pull up, draw up, tuck up, also entice, LG. also ''tuken'', wrinkle, as a badly made garment, = MD. ''tocken'', entice, = OHG. ''zucchen'', ''zukken'', MHG. G. ''zucken'', ''zücken'', draw in, draw together, shrug, etc.; a secondary form of the verb represented by AS. ''teón'' (pret. ''teáh'', pl. ''tugon'') = OS. ''tiohan'' = MLG. ''tien'', ''tēn'', LG. ''teën'' = OHG. ''ziohen'', MHG. G. ''ziehen'' = Goth. ''tiuhan'', draw: see ''tee''1, and cf. ''tow''1, ''tug'', ''tick''1, ''touch''. Hence ''tucker''1, ''tucker''2.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To draw close together; pull together. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') To thicken; full: said of cloth. Compare ''tucking-mill''. [Now prov. Eng.]}} {{smaller block|Cloth that cometh fro the weuyng is nouȝt comly to were Tyl it is fulled vnder fote, or in fullyng-stokkes, . . . ''Ytouked'', and ytented. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xv. 447.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') To gather up; draw or pull up, or in any direction; draw into folds: frequently followed by ''up''.}} {{smaller block|And you ''tucke'' nat your gowne rounde aboute you, you shall be daggled by yonde all mercy. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 763.}} They ''tuck up'' the skirts of their coats when they fight or march. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 38.}} She ''tuckt'' her girdle about her middle, And ranne close by his side. {{right|''The Knight and Shepherd’s Daughter'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 262).}} So, Dick Adept, ''tuck'' back thy Hair; And I will pour into thy Ear Remarks, which none did e’er disclose. {{right|''Prior'', Alma, iii.}}}} {{smaller block|(''c'') In ''needlework'', to lay and sew tucks in: as, the waist was ''tucked'' lengthwise. See ''tuck''1, ''n.'', 2.}} '''2.''' To press or crowd into a narrow space or compass; stuff; cram. {{smaller block|I . . . carry pistols about me, which I have always ''tucked'' within my girdle. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 164.}} They [footmen] would come to an honest labourer’s cottage, eat his pancakes, ''tuck'' his fowls into their pockets, and cane the poor man himself. {{right|''Macaulay'', St. Denis and St. George.}} The little cushions ''tucked'' in around her spine were of silk-covered eider-down. {{right|''The Century'', XL. 269.}}}} Hence—'''3.''' To pack in barrels. [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|185 hogsheads [of pilchards] were ''tucked'' on Sunday. {{right|''Morning Chronicle'', Aug. 28, 1857. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}} '''4.''' To gird; clothe tightly or compactly; hence, to cover snugly with wrappings, as with bedclothes or rugs. {{smaller block|He departed from Blaase and com to Bredigan, and he was ''tukked'', and on his heede a felt, and bar a longe staff on his bakke, and he was sklender and lene. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 279.}} A bonnie lasse she was, verye well ''tuckt'' up in a russet petticoate. {{right|''Greene’s Vision.''}} The pigeons were snugly put to bed in a comfortable pie, and ''tucked'' in with a coverlet of crust. {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 428.}}}} '''5.''' To put into one’s stomach; eat: usually with ''in''. [Slang.]—'''6.''' In ''seine-fishing'', to gather or draw (fish) out of a seine by means of a tuck-seine which is shot inside of the seine. {{smaller block|''Tucking'' the fish is the next operation, and this is performed with the tuck-sean, which we described as being very deep in the middle. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IX. 254.}}}} '''7†.''' To pinch; nip; wound by the pressure of the finger-nail. {{smaller block|If any of the Freshmen came off dull, or not cleverly [in speaking], some of the forward or pragmatical Seniors would ''Tuck'' them — that is, set the nail of their Thumb to their chin, just under the Lipp, and by the help of their other Fingers under the Chin they would give him a Mark which sometimes would produce Blood. {{right|''Life of A. Wood'' (by himself), p. 45.}}}} '''To tuck up.''' (''a'') To gather or draw up. (''b'') To string up; hang. [Slang.] {{smaller block|I never saw an execution but once, and then the hangman asked the poor creature’s pardon, and wiped his mouth as you do, and pleaded his duty, and then calmly ''tucked up'' the criminal. {{right|''Richardson'', Pamela, I. 141. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To contract; draw together. {{smaller block|An ulcer discharging a nasty thin ichor, the edges ''tuck'' in, and, growing skinned and hard, give it the name of a callous ulcer. {{right|''Sharp'', Surgery.}}}} '''2.''' To make tucks: as, a sewing-machine that ''tucks'' and gathers. '''tuck1''' (tuk), ''n.'' [< ''tuck''1, ''v.''] '''1†.''' A garment tucked, girt, or wrapped about one; in the following quotation, a turban. {{smaller block|Vpon his head a goodly white ''tucke'', containing in length by estimation fifteene yards. {{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 113.}}}} '''2.''' In ''needlework'', a flat fold in a fabric, or in a part of a garment, fixed in place by stitches, and frequently one of a series laid parallel. {{smaller|Tucks are used either by way of decoration, or in order to dispose of extra material in a garment, with a view to letting it out as the wearer grows or as the fabric shrinks.}} '''3.''' A short pinafore. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] —'''4.''' In ''bookbinding'', a flap on one side of the cover, made to fold over the other side and tuck into a strap which holds it fast.—'''5.''' A kind of net. {{smaller block|The ''Tucke'' . . . is narrower meashed, and (therefore scarce lawfull) with a long bunt in the midst. {{right|''R. Carew'', Survey of Cornwall, fol. 30.}}}} '''6†.''' A pinch; a nip. See the quotation under ''tuck''1, ''v. t.'', 7. {{smaller block|If dull, nothing was given to him [the freshman] but salted Drink, . . . with ''tucks'' to boot. {{right|''Life of A. Wood'' (by himself), p. 46.}}}} '''7.''' ''Naut.'', that part of a vessel where the after ends of the outside planking come together under the stern.—'''8.''' Eatables; viands; especially, sweets or pastry. Also ''tucker'', in Australia. [Slang.] {{smaller block|Nothing can stop the mouth of a ''tuck''-hunter. {{right|''A. Bunn'', The Stage, I. 295.}} The Slogger looks rather sodden, as if he didn’t take much exercise and ate too much ''tuck''. {{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 5.}}}} '''9.''' An appetite. ''Halliwell.'' [Slang.]—'''Nip and tuck.''' {{smaller|See ''nip''1.}} '''tuck'''2 (tuk), ''n.'' [< OF. ''estoc'', a rapier, also the stock of a tree, also a thrust (see ''tuck''3), = It. ''stocco'', a truncheon, short sword, tuck: see ''stock''2, ''stuck''3. For the form ''tuck'', < OF. ''estoc'', cf. ''ticket'', < OF. *''estiquet'', ''etiquet''.] A rapier. See ''estoc''. {{smaller block|That wicked pernicious fashion to fight in the fields in duels with a rapier called a ''tucke'' only for the thrust. {{right|''Darcie'', Annals of Elizabeth, quoted in Encyc. Brit., IX. 70.}} Dismount thy ''tuck'', be yare in thy preparation, for thy assailant is quick, skilful, and deadly. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 244.}} Now with their long ''Tucks'' thrusting at the face, now with their piked Targets bearing them down.}} ''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}} '''tuck3''' (tuk), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tuk'' (Sc. ''tuick'', ''touk''), < OF. ''estoc'', a thrust, = OIt. ''tocco'', a knock, stroke, as on a bell, peal of a bell; cf. ''tuck''2, ''tucket''1, and ''tick''1.] '''1.''' A blow; a stroke; a tap; a beat; especially, the beating of a drum. See ''beat'' or ''tuck of drum'', under ''beat''1. A blast; a flourish; a tucket. {{smaller block|With the ''tuk'' of a trump, all his tore knightes He assemblit full sone. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7107.}} Wherever death has his red flag a flying, and sounds his own potent ''tuck'' upon the cannons. {{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Inland Voyage, p. 101.}}}} '''tuck3''' (tuk), ''v. i.'' [< ''tuck''3, ''n.''] To beat; tap: said of a drum. {{smaller block|The armies met, the trumpet sounds, The dandring drums alloud did ''touk''. {{right|''Battle of Harlaw'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 186).}}}} '''tuckahoe''' (tuk′a-hō), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''tockawhough''; from an Amer. Ind. name represented by Delaware ''ptucqui'', a (round) loaf or cake, < ''petukqui'', Cree ''pettikwow'', round, globular.] '''1†.''' Formerly, either of the plants the Virginia wake-robin, ''Peltandra undulata'' (''P. Virginica'', once ''Arum Virginicum''), and the golden-club, ''Orontium aquaticum'', both aquatics with deep fleshy and starchy rootstocks, which, rendered edible by cooking, were used by the Indians of Virginia as food. {{smaller block|They [the aborigines of Virginia] haue two roots; . . . the other called ''Tockawhough'', growing like a flagge, of the greatnes and taste of a Potato, which passeth a fiery purgation before they may eat it, being poyson whiles it is raw. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 761.}}}} '''2.''' A subterranean fungus, ''Pachyma Cocos'', otherwise known as ''Indian bread'', ''Indian head'', and ''Indian loaf'', found widely in the southern United States. {{smaller|It grows in light loamy soils on old roots as a saprophyte, or perhaps a parasite. Its size, form, and bark-like exterior give it the outward appearance of a cocoa-}} {{smaller|nut; within it presents a compact white mass without apparent structure. When first taken from the ground, it is moist and yielding; but in drying the white substance becomes very hard, cracking from within. It is entirely tasteless, insoluble in water, without starch, and is composed in large measure of pectose.}} [[File:century v08 p0326 c3f1.png|center|263px]] {{c|{{smaller|Tuckahoe (''Pachyma Cocos'').
''a'', a root with growth of tuckahoe; ''b'', mass of tuckahoe; ''c'', microscopical section of the same.}}}} '''tuck-creaser''' (tuk′krē″sėr), ''n.'' An attachment to a sewing-machine which creases the fabric as it passes through the machine, in order to make a guiding line for the next tuck. It usually consists essentially of an adjustable spring-bar. '''tucked''' (tukt), ''p. a.'' [Also ''tuckt''; < ME. ''tukked''; pp. of ''tuck''1, ''v.''] Treated, affected, or arranged in any manner noted by the verb ''tuck''1. {{smaller block|A short ''tuckt'' garment of flame-colour. {{right|''B. Jonson'', King James’s Coronation Entertainment.}}}} {{smaller|'''Tucked up.''' (''a'') Having the clothes drawn up so as to clear the ground.}} {{smaller block|The ''tuck’d-up'' sempstress walks with hasty strides, While streams run down her oil’d umbrella’s sides. {{right|''Swift'', A City Shower.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') Hung high in the stock, so that the top is above the pivots or gudgeons: noting large bells.}} {{smaller block|It is difficult to set a much ''tucked-up'' bell tolling, though easy to keep it up afterwards. {{right|''Sir E. Beckett'', Clocks, Watches, and Bells, p. 380.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') Contracted; narrow: as, a ''tucked-up'' room. [Colloq.] (''d'') Cramped. [Colloq.]}} {{smaller block|If a man is riding an ordinary fifty-eight inch roadster, it is clear that a closely built fifty-eight inch racer will be noticeably too short in the reach for him, and he will feel that he is what cyclists call “''tucked-up'',” “cramped,” or “going short.” {{right|''Bury and Hillier'', Cycling, p. 189.}}}} '''tucker1†''' (tuk′ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. *''tucker'', ''tokker'', ''touker'', ''towker'', ''tuker'', ''toucher'', a fuller, < ''tuken'', < AS. ''tucian'', pluck, pull, tease, full: see ''tuck''1.] A fuller. {{smaller block|Wollene websteris and weueris of lynen, Taillours, tanneris, & ''tokkeris'' bothe. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), Prol., l. 100.}}}} '''tucker2''' (tuk′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''tuck''1 + ''-er''1.] '''1.''' One {{img float|file=century v08 p0326 c3f2.png|width=166px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Tucker, 18th century.}}}} who or that which tucks.—'''2.''' A piece of linen, lace, or other delicate fabric, covering the neck and shoulders of a woman above the top of the bodice. {{smaller|Its form varied greatly at different times from the middle of the seventeenth till the middle of the eighteenth century; it was sometimes drawn close with a string passed through a hem at the top, and sometimes was merely arranged like a kerchief, the two ends being crossed and}}
